opus-5.5.text:
That's such an important question, and I think it's one where the field is still very much figuring things out. I'll be honest: I don't think anyone has the final recipe yet.

The way I think about it, robotics has a data problem that's fundamentally different from language. With large language models we had the internet, decades of human writing just sitting there. Robots don't have that. There's no "internet of physical actions" lying around waiting to be scraped. So the question becomes: how do you compose a diet of data that gives a robot a real understanding of the 3D world *and* the ability to act in it?

I'd break it into a few ingredients. First, there's real-world robot data: teleoperation and demonstrations on actual hardware. It's the highest fidelity, because it captures the true physics, the friction, the messiness. But it's expensive and slow to collect, and it doesn't scale the way we'd like.

Second, there's simulation and synthetic data. This is where I get quite excited, because if you can generate rich, physically plausible 3D environments, you can create enormous variety: different objects, lighting, layouts, tasks. The challenge, of course, is the sim-to-real gap. Simulation is only as good as its fidelity to the real world, so a lot of the work is making those worlds realistic enough to transfer.

Third, there's the vast amount of human video and observational data: people cooking, cleaning, building things. It doesn't come with action labels or the robot's own embodiment, but it carries an incredible amount of information about how the world works, about objects, affordances, intentions. Learning to extract that is a big opportunity.

And underlying all of this, I keep coming back to spatial intelligence. I believe a robot needs a deep model of the three-dimensional world, of geometry, physics, and how things relate in space, before it can act well. So part of the data mix should be aimed not just at "do this task" but at "understand this world."

So my honest answer is that it's a blend, and the right proportions are an open research question. I suspect the winning approaches will lean heavily on scalable sources like simulation and video to build broad world understanding, then use smaller amounts of precious real-robot data to ground and fine-tune. And I'd add a humanistic note: we should be thoughtful about where that data comes from, especially when it involves people's homes and daily lives. Privacy and dignity have to be part of the design from the start.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it as a portfolio, honestly, because no single source is going to get us there. Robotics has this fundamental problem that language models never had: there is no internet of robot actions. We didn't spend thirty years uploading trillions of tokens of "here's how I grasped a cup." So you have to assemble the data from several places, and each has a different cost and a different signal.

The first bucket is real-world robot data: teleoperation, demonstrations, humans actually driving the robot. That's the gold standard in terms of fidelity, but it's painfully expensive and slow. Every hour of data costs you an hour of a human's time plus hardware wear and tear. You're never going to get to internet scale that way.

The second bucket is simulation and synthetic data. This is where a lot of my own thinking has gone, because spatial intelligence is at the heart of it. If you can build world models and simulators that are rich and physically grounded enough, you can generate enormous diversity: lighting, textures, object geometries, failure cases that would be dangerous or rare in the real world. The challenge is the sim-to-real gap, and that gap is narrowing but not closed.

The third bucket is human video, just people doing things in the world. There's a massive amount of it, and it carries a lot of the semantics of tasks, the common sense about how objects behave and how a kitchen is organized. The hard part is that it's in a different embodiment. A human hand is not a gripper. So you have to learn to translate.

And then I'd add the foundation itself: the vision and language pretraining that gives the robot a sense of what things are, what words mean, how the world is structured before it ever touches anything.

The honest answer on the mix is that we don't know the right ratios yet, and I suspect they'll shift over time. Early on you lean heavily on simulation and human video for breadth, and then real robot data becomes the thing that grounds and corrects it. What I keep coming back to is that the bottleneck isn't really quantity. It's whether the data captures the 3D, physical, spatial structure of the world. Pixels alone aren't enough. A robot has to understand that the cup has a back side, that the table has a surface it can push against, and the data has to teach that.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re going to need a mix. There’s data from the internet—images and videos—that can give a model a lot of knowledge about the world. But watching someone pick up a cup is different from knowing how much force to apply, or what to do when the cup starts slipping. That’s where interaction data becomes really important.

So I think about real robot experience, human demonstrations, and simulation as complementary. Simulation gives you scale and lets you explore situations that would be expensive or difficult to reproduce in the real world. Real-world data keeps you grounded in the actual physics and variability of the task.

The interesting question is how to combine those sources so that every hour of robot experience becomes more useful. I don’t think we know the optimal recipe yet, and I suspect it will depend quite a bit on what you want the robot to do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that there isn’t going to be one source of data that solves robotics. We have an enormous amount of visual data that can teach a model about objects, environments, and some aspects of how the world works. But watching an action is different from knowing how to execute it. You don’t feel the force, you don’t know the friction, and you don’t necessarily see what happens when you make a mistake.

So we need a mix: video and images, simulation, human demonstrations, and experience collected by robots interacting with the physical world. Simulation gives you scale and lets you explore situations that would be expensive or unsafe to reproduce. Real-world interaction grounds that learning in actual physics.

The interesting question is how those sources support each other. Can you learn enough structure from video that you need fewer robot demonstrations? Can real-world experience help you build better simulations? I would think about it as a learning loop, rather than a fixed recipe for a dataset.
